Newly hatched Bluefin killifish emerge from the egg at a total length of approximately 0.6 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.6 centimeters], a diminutive size characteristic of many fundulids. These alevin, or yolk-sac larvae, are lecithotrophic and depend entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-hatching. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the period from fertilization to hatching lasts about 7.8 days [ab = about 7.8 days]; this incubation duration is consistent with other small-bodied cyprinodontiforms and reflects the rapid developmental rates permitted by warm, stable thermal environments. As the larvae progress through the yolk-sac resorption phase, they begin exogenous feeding upon the completion of yolk absorption. The onset of first feeding marks a critical transition to the free-swimming, planktonic larval stage during which growth is rapid. Under the stable 25 °C [T = 25 °C] thermal regime, individuals achieve a total length at puberty of 2.3 centimeters [Lp = 2.3 centimeters], a size at which gametogenesis begins and individuals become reproductively viable. Body mass at this pivotal developmental milestone is approximately 0.09 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.09 grams], a weight that represents a substantial increase from the neonatal stage and indicates significant investment in somatic growth prior to the onset of reproductive allocation. Females produce approximately 2 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2 eggs per spawning event], with nearly continuous spawning capable of yielding around 100 clutches per year [F_R_i = around 100 clutches per year], reflecting the species' capacity for sustained reproduction under favorable conditions.

The ultimate or asymptotic total length for Bluefin killifish has been recorded at 6.0 centimeters [Li = 6.0 centimeters], a modest maximum size that places this species among the smaller members of the Fundulidae family. This terminal length is reached after a period of sustained growth under optimal thermal conditions. Associated with this adult size is an ultimate wet weight of 1.65 grams [Wwi = 1.65 grams], derived from length-weight regressions that have been validated across multiple populations. Sexual dimorphism is minimal, although gravid females may temporarily exceed this mass due to the accumulation of developing oocytes. The species' iteroparous reproductive strategy, combined with its relatively small body size, dictates a life history characterized by high fecundity and comparatively early maturation, enabling populations to persist in variable and often ephemeral freshwater habitats throughout the southeastern United States.

In a stable thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum lifespan observed for Bluefin killifish from the time of hatching until natural death is approximately 730 days [am = approximately 730 days], equivalent to two full years. This relatively short longevity is typical of small-bodied annual or biannual fishes and reflects a life history strategy that prioritizes rapid maturation and high reproductive output over extended somatic persistence. Mortality in the wild is also heavily influenced by predation pressure and seasonal habitat drying, which truncate lifespan considerably compared to protected laboratory conditions. The species' capacity to complete its life cycle within a single year ensures population resilience in unpredictable environments. Post-reproductive senescence, if it occurs under natural conditions, is likely brief given the intense selective pressures favoring semelparous or near-semelparous breeding schedules in ephemeral water bodies.

The estimated daily reproduction rate of this species is approximately 0.575 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.575 eggs per day] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a value derived from the product of clutch size and clutch frequency under continuous spawning conditions. This high reproductive capacity is facilitated by the female's ability to continuously recruit oocytes from the ovarian germinal epithelium, a trait shared with other fundulids. Comparative life history data show that the wet weight at puberty of 0.09 grams [Wwp = 0.09 grams] is reached well before the ultimate body size is achieved, allowing for a prolonged reproductive window that overlaps substantially with continued somatic growth. Field surveys corroborate that populations in thermally stable springs often maintain continuous reproduction throughout the year, while those in more seasonal habitats exhibit distinct spawning peaks coinciding with spring and early summer rains.
